title: Quantum Reservoir Computing
intro: Quantum reservoir computing uses the natural dynamics of a quantum system as a fixed, untrained memory for signals that unfold in time, and trains only a simple linear readout on what is measured. This shelf teaches it from the beginning, in six chapters: the machine learning it needs, the classical theory, the open-system quantum mechanics, the models, the hardware, and what is known about its power and limits.

blocks.text: Variables and symbols

The symbols used across this shelf. Reservoir computing borrows letters from machine learning, dynamical systems and quantum information, so many of them have more than one meaning; every meaning is listed, numbered, with the setting it belongs to. Highlight a symbol on any page of the shelf to see its meanings. The symbols of the underlying quantum mechanics are listed on the Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum) shelf. If you are new, skip this table for now and come back to it when a page uses a letter you do not recognise.
Inputs, targets and time

items: $u_k,\ u(t)$: the input at step $k$ on the classical reservoir pages; $u(t)$ is an input applied as a continuous drive.
$s_k$: the input at step $k$ on the quantum pages, $s_k\in[0,1]$, because it sets a qubit amplitude.
$k$: the time step: the $k$-th input, with $\rho_k$ and $x_k$ the state and features after it.
$y_k,\ \hat y_k$: the target at step $k$; $\hat y_k$ is the readout's prediction of it.

$T,\ T_0,\ \mathcal{T}_s$: (1) the length of a time series (number of input steps); $T_0$ is the washout and $T_{\mathrm{test}}$ the number of test points; (2) $\mathcal{T}_{s}$: the input-dependent channel applied at each step, $\rho_k = \mathcal{T}_{s_k}(\rho_{k-1})$; (3) for a qubit channel: the $3\times3$ matrix in its Bloch map $\vec r\mapsto T\vec r + \vec t$; (4) in a delay reservoir: the response time of the nonlinear node.
$T_1,\ T_2,\ T_\varphi$: $T_1$ is the relaxation (energy-decay) time, $T_2$ the coherence time and $T_\varphi$ the pure-dephasing time, related by $1/T_2 = 1/(2T_1) + 1/T_\varphi$.
$\Delta t$: the time the reservoir evolves between two inputs.
$d$: (1) a delay: the memory function $r^2(d)$ scores recall of the input $d$ steps back; (2) the dimension of a Hilbert space; an input state on $d$ dimensions has $d^2$ operators.
$L,\ L_j,\ \mathcal{L}$: (1) a number of past inputs: a window of the last $L$ steps; (2) $L_j$: the jump operators of a Lindblad equation, and $\mathcal{L}$ the Liouvillian.
$w$: (1) the readout weight vector, the only thing learned; (2) the memory window: a restart only needs the last $w$ inputs.

$\tau$: (1) a delay: the $\tau = 17$ in the Mackey-Glass equation, or a delay reservoir's feedback delay ($\tau_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the time an input is held); (2) a memory time: two copies of a reservoir approach by $e^{-1/\tau}$ per step; (3) the time a Hamiltonian encoding acts, $e^{-i(H_0 + sH_1)\tau}$.
$\theta$: (1) in a delay reservoir: the spacing of virtual nodes along the delay; (2) an encoding angle, $\theta_k = 2\arcsin\sqrt{s_k}$ in $R_Y(\theta_k)$.
$\mathrm{MC}$: linear memory capacity; NMSE: mean squared error divided by the target variance (both in the glossary under their names).

blocks.text: Classical reservoirs and the readout

items: $x_k$: the feature vector (reservoir state) at step $k$; $x_{k,i}$ is its $i$-th feature, $\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho_k)$ for a quantum reservoir.
$x,\ p$: (1) a single feature value, such as $\langle Z_i\rangle = x$ estimated from shots; (2) for an oscillator: the position quadrature, with $p$ the momentum.

$N$: (1) the number of reservoir units (features) in an echo state network; (2) for an oscillator: the Fock-space truncation, keeping levels $0$ to $N-1$; (3) $N_{\mathrm{ens}}$: the number of identical copies in an ensemble readout.

$W,\ W_{\mathrm{in}},\ W_{\mathrm{out}}$: (1) the recurrent weight matrix of an echo state network ($N\times N$, random); $W_{\mathrm{in}}$ holds the input weights and $W_{\mathrm{out}}$ the trained readout; (2) for a spin reservoir: the disorder strength, with random fields drawn from $[-W/2, W/2]$.

$\rho$: (1) the density matrix of the reservoir; $\rho_k$ is the state after input $k$ and $\rho_{01}$ a matrix element; (2) $\rho(W)$: the spectral radius of an ESN weight matrix, its largest eigenvalue modulus.
$a$: (1) the leak rate of an echo state network; (2) for an oscillator: the annihilation operator, with $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$.

$K,\ K_m$: (1) the input dimension of an echo state network, $u_k\in\mathbb{R}^K$; (2) the Kerr strength of a nonlinear oscillator, $K\,a^\dagger a\,a^\dagger a$; (3) the number of reservoirs run in parallel (spatial multiplexing); (4) $K_m$: the Kraus operators of a channel, $\rho\mapsto\sum_m K_m\rho K_m^\dagger$.

$\lambda$: (1) the ridge regularisation strength, in $(Z^\top Z + \lambda I)^{-1}$; (2) eigenvalues: $\lambda_i$ of $W$ (the spectral radius is $\max_i\vert\lambda_i\vert$) or $\lambda_k$ of the Liouvillian; (3) $\lambda_1$: the largest conditional Lyapunov exponent; the echo state property needs $\lambda_1 < 0$.

$\sigma$: (1) singular values: $\sigma_i$ of the feature matrix, and $\sigma_{\max}(W)$ the largest singular value of $W$; (2) a standard deviation or noise level: input variance $\sigma_u^2$, feature noise variance $\sigma^2$, or the width of a weak-measurement pointer; (3) a second density matrix, as in the trace distance $D(\rho, \sigma)$; (4) $\sigma^\pm$: the qubit raising and lowering operators in amplitude damping; (5) for oscillators: the covariance matrix $\sigma_{jk}$ of a Gaussian state.
$Z$: (1) the feature matrix: feature vectors stacked as rows, $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times M}$; (2) the Pauli $Z$ operator; $\langle Z_i\rangle$ on each qubit is the usual set of features.
$Y$: the target matrix: targets stacked as rows to match $Z$.
$F$: (1) the reservoir map, $x_k = F(x_{k-1}, u_k)$; (2) the feature matrix in the ridge solution $w = (F^\top F + \lambda I)^{-1}F^\top y$.
$M,\ M_m$: (1) the number of features the readout uses; (2) $M_m$: measurement operators, with $\sum_m M_m^\dagger M_m = I$.

$r$: (1) $r^2(d)$: the squared correlation between the readout and the input $d$ steps back (the memory function); (2) $r_\mu = \operatorname{Tr}(P_\mu\rho)$: the Pauli coordinates of a state (its generalised Bloch vector); (3) $r_k$: the squeezing magnitude used to encode an input in an oscillator.
$C$: (1) a capacity: $C_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total information processing capacity and $C[z]$ the capacity for one target $z$; (2) the concurrence of a two-qubit state.

$m$: (1) in a delay reservoir: the mask values $m_1,\dots,m_N$ that set each virtual node's input weight; (2) a number of qubits an input is re-uploaded into, or of ancilla qubits; (3) a measurement outcome label, as in $M_m$ and $p_m$.
$b$: (1) random bits $b_k$ in the parity task; (2) the input-dependent shift in a state-affine reservoir, $r_k = A(s_k)r_{k-1} + b(s_k)$.
$A(s)$: the input-dependent matrix of a state-affine reservoir, $r_k = A(s_k)r_{k-1} + b(s_k)$.
$G$: a target filter, $y_k = G(s_k, s_{k-1}, \dots)$: causal, time-invariant and with fading memory.

blocks.text: Quantum reservoirs and measurement

items: $n,\ n_i$: (1) the number of qubits in the reservoir; (2) the order of a NARMA task (NARMA$n$) or of an $n$-bit parity; (3) in a Rydberg array: the occupation $n_i = (1 - Z_i)/2$ of atom $i$.
$S$: the number of shots per feature; shot noise falls as $1/\sqrt{S}$.
$V,\ V_{ij}$: (1) the number of virtual nodes: the times the reservoir is read between two inputs; (2) in a Rydberg array: the van der Waals interaction $V_{ij}\propto 1/r_{ij}^6$.

$O_i,\ O_w,\ O(\cdot)$: (1) $O_i$: the observables read out, so feature $i$ is $\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho_k)$; (2) $O_w = \sum_k w_kE_k$: the single observable a trained QELM readout amounts to; (3) $O(\cdot)$: order of growth, as in a cost of $O(ST^2)$.

$E_m,\ E_k,\ \mathcal{E}$: (1) $E_m$: POVM elements, $E_m = M_m^\dagger M_m$, with $p_m = \operatorname{Tr}(E_m\rho)$; (2) $E_k$: an effective POVM, the measurement pulled back through the reservoir, $E_k = \mathcal{E}^\dagger(\Pi_k)$; (3) $E_k$: energy levels, whose gaps give the level statistics; (4) $\mathcal{E}$: a quantum channel.
$J,\ J_{ij}$: (1) the couplings $J_{ij}$ of a spin reservoir, drawn at scale $J$; (2) $J_k$: the Jacobian of the driven map at step $k$; (3) $J(\mathcal{E})$: the Choi matrix of a channel.
$h,\ h_i$: the field on each qubit of a spin reservoir, $h_i = h + \delta_i$.

$\delta$: (1) $\delta_i$: the random offsets of the fields in a disordered spin reservoir; (2) a detuning between two spins, $\delta = h_1 - h_2$, which limits how far an excitation hops; (3) a failure probability: all estimates are within $\epsilon$ with probability $1-\delta$.

$\Delta$: (1) in a Rydberg array: the detunings $\Delta_i$; (2) $\Delta(\rho)$: the map that removes all coherences in the computational basis (full dephasing); (3) for an oscillator: the detuning in $\Delta\,a^\dagger a$.
$\Omega$: in a Rydberg array: the Rabi drive on each atom.

$\gamma$: (1) a decay rate: amplitude damping at $\gamma = 1/T_1$, or the rate $\gamma_j$ of jump operator $L_j$; (2) the amplitude-damping probability per step in a channel's Kraus form; (3) the decay coefficient in the Mackey-Glass equation.
$\kappa$: the photon-loss rate of an oscillator.
$\eta$: (1) the contraction coefficient of a channel: the most it can keep the trace distance between two states; (2) noise added to the features, of variance $\sigma^2$.

$\epsilon,\ \varepsilon$: (1) a target precision: the number of shots grows as $\epsilon^{-2}$; (2) the strength of a weak measurement, from $0$ (nothing learned) to $1$ (projective); (3) the input drive amplitude of an oscillator reservoir.
$\alpha$: (1) the input scaling of the drive in a Kerr oscillator reservoir, $\alpha\,u(t)(a + a^\dagger)$; (2) the amplitude of a coherent state $\vert\alpha\rangle$.
$\beta$: the feedback coefficient in the Mackey-Glass equation.
$\mu$: an index over Pauli strings, as in $\rho = 2^{-n}(I + \sum_\mu r_\mu P_\mu)$.

$p$: (1) the strength of depolarising noise per step, $\rho\mapsto(1-p)\rho + pI/2^n$; (2) a probability: $p_m$ or $p_k$ of a measurement outcome; (3) the exponent $p = 10$ in the Mackey-Glass equation.
$D$: (1) the trace distance $D(\rho, \sigma) = \tfrac12\Vert\rho - \sigma\Vert_1$; (2) the Hilbert-space dimension $D = 2^n$; $I/D$ is the maximally mixed state.
$g$: (1) the Liouvillian gap: the slowest rate at which the state approaches its steady state; (2) $g_k = E_{k+1} - E_k$: the gaps between neighbouring energy levels.
$P_\mu,\ P_n$: (1) $P_\mu$: a Pauli string; (2) $P_n$: the population of Fock state $\vert n\rangle$.
$U$: (1) the unitary applied in one reservoir step; (2) $\mathcal{U}[a, b]$: the uniform distribution on $[a, b]$, used to draw random couplings.
$\Pi$: (1) the parity $\Pi = Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$, conserved by the spin-network reservoir; (2) $\Pi_m$: projectors of a projective measurement.
$I$: the identity; $I/D$ (or $I/2^n$) is the maximally mixed state.
$c$: the contraction factor per step: distances shrink as $c^k$, so $c^{d_{\max}}$ should be small for the longest delay needed.
$\phi_k$: the squeezing phase used to encode an input in an oscillator.
$\xi$: the coherence term of the reset encoding, $\xi = \sqrt{s(1-s)}$; with one upload every feature depends on each input through $1$, $s$ and $\xi$.
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}$: the effective number of features, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}(S) \approx \sum_i \sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2 + 1/S)$: how many feature directions stand above the shot noise.
$\gamma_a$: on the Quantum Advantage page, the Majorana operators of the Jordan-Wigner mapping ($a = 0, \dots, 2n-1$); elsewhere $\gamma$ is a decay rate or probability (see $\gamma$).

blocks.text: What this shelf is

Many things we want to predict unfold in time: the next value of a sensor, tomorrow's demand, the next sample of a signal. A computer that handles them has to remember the recent past and combine it in nonlinear ways. Reservoir computing gets that memory almost for free: it drives a fixed dynamical system with the input, lets the system's own dynamics hold a fading trace of the past, and trains only a simple weighted sum on top. Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) uses a quantum system, a handful of interacting qubits or a few modes of light, as that fixed dynamical system.

This shelf teaches the subject from the beginning. It does not assume you know machine learning or quantum mechanics beyond school algebra and the idea of a derivative. Every page opens with what it assumes and what you will be able to do afterwards, builds each idea step by step with numbers, ends its main sections with a short 'Check yourself' question, and closes with problems whose solutions are written out in full. Most pages also have a code sample (numpy only) whose output is quoted on the page, and many have an interactive plot.
The idea in one paragraph

A recurrent network has to be trained through time, which is slow and unstable. Reservoir computing (Jaeger's echo state networks and Maass's liquid state machines, both 2001–2002) separates the job: a fixed, randomly built dynamical system (the reservoir) is driven by the input, its state becomes a rich nonlinear record of the recent input history, and only a linear readout is trained, by ridge regression in one shot. Anything with the right dynamics can be the reservoir: a bucket of water, a laser with delayed feedback, a spintronic oscillator. Fujii and Nakajima (2017) proposed a quantum one: a register of interacting qubits whose Hilbert space grows as $2^n$, read out through expectation values.

blocks.caption: The whole of QRC: a quantum channel that depends on the input drives the state; measured expectations are the features; only the linear readout w is trained.

blocks.text: For this to work as a reservoir the input-driven channel must forget its initial state (the echo state property, which in the quantum case requires the input-driven channels to contract the distance between states, at least over several steps, so a closed unitary system alone never qualifies); it must mix past inputs nonlinearly; and the features must be estimated from a finite number of measurement shots, each of which disturbs or destroys the state. Those three facts organise most of the field.
The chapters, in order
There are six chapters. Read them in this order the first time; each one's front page explains its pages and the order to read them in.

items: Getting Started (#/qrc/start) (six pages, about six to ten hours). The machine learning the rest of the shelf assumes, taught from zero: what reservoir computing is (no maths), time series and prediction, a neural network computed by hand, linear regression and the ridge readout derived step by step, training and testing with NMSE, and finally a complete two-qubit quantum reservoir worked by hand, three time steps with every density matrix written out. Start here even if you know some physics.

Reservoir Computing Foundations (#/qrc/foundations) (five pages, about five to ten hours). The classical theory made exact: echo state networks, the echo state property (why a reservoir must forget where it started), memory capacity and information processing capacity (how much of the past a readout can recover), physical reservoirs such as water and light, and the benchmark tasks every paper reports.

Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems) (four pages, about nine hours). The quantum mechanics past the basics that a reservoir runs on: density matrices and channels, the Lindblad equation for decay and dephasing, contraction (the quantum form of the echo state property), and measurement and its cost in shots.

Quantum Reservoir Models (#/qrc/models) (eight pages, about eight to ten hours). The model families one at a time: the spin-network reservoir that started the field, how an input is written into qubits, readouts and multiplexing, the dynamical regimes in which a reservoir computes well, dissipation as a resource, continuous-variable reservoirs, quantum extreme learning machines and tasks whose inputs are quantum states.

Measurement and Hardware (#/qrc/hardware) (five pages, about four to five hours). What changes on a real device: measurement back-action and shot noise, online measurement protocols, gate-based and analog platforms, and an honest count of runs, shots and seconds.

Theory, Limits and Practice (#/qrc/theory) (five pages, about eight to ten hours). What a quantum reservoir can and cannot compute, why adding qubits does not automatically add usable features, what a quantum advantage would have to mean and how to test for one fairly, a complete simulator in numpy, and the open problems.

blocks.text: All together that is roughly 40 to 55 hours of study, more if you work every problem and run every sample. Short sittings of one page each work well; the pages are written to be read one at a time.
Three ways through

items: New to both fields: read the chapters in the order above. Before the last page of Getting Started (#/qrc/start), or whenever a page uses qubits, density matrices or measurement, read the matching pages of the Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum) shelf; each QRC page names the ones it needs in its first lines.

You know machine learning but not quantum mechanics: skim the first five pages of Getting Started (#/qrc/start), work through the Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum) shelf up to mixed states, then read A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand) and continue from Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems).

You know quantum mechanics but not machine learning: read Getting Started (#/qrc/start) in full (it is where the machine-learning ideas are taught), skim Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems), and go on from Quantum Reservoir Models (#/qrc/models).

blocks.text: If you only have an afternoon: What Is Reservoir Computing? (#/qrc/start/what-is-reservoir-computing), then A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand), then The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir) with its live simulator, then Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability) for the main limit on how far it scales.
Key equations of the shelf
Besides the update rule above, these are the equations the shelf keeps coming back to. Each line says what it means; the page named after it derives it.

blocks.caption: The ridge readout: the weights that best fit the targets $y$ from the table $X$ of features, with a penalty $\lambda$ that keeps them small. Page: Linear Regression and the Ridge Readout.
The score: 0 is perfect, 1 is no better than predicting the average. Page: Training, Testing and Measuring Error.

Memory capacity adds up how well the input $d$ steps back can be recovered; the total capacity over all targets is at most the number $N$ of independent features. Page: Memory and Processing Capacity.
Contraction: if every input channel shrinks the trace distance by a factor $\eta < 1$, the reservoir forgets its initial state, which is the echo state property. Page: Contraction and Fixed Points.

Every feature is an average of $S$ outcomes of $\pm1$, with this error; and under fully scrambling dynamics a Pauli feature's spread over inputs shrinks with the number of qubits $n$ like this. Pages: Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise, Concentration and Scalability.

blocks.text: Conventions used on every page: $\hbar = 1$ (energies and frequencies in the same units); $\vert 0\rangle$ is the state with $Z = +1$; in a tensor product the leftmost factor is qubit 1, the qubit the input is written into; $H$ is a Hamiltonian and $H_d$ the Hadamard gate.
The interactive plots on this shelf run an exact density-matrix simulation of a 2- to 5-qubit reservoir in your browser, so every number they show comes from the real model, not a sketch.
